item.title: Where in the world is whitlockite
item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02097-9

Whitlockite can trace ancient impacts in space, human activity at archaeological sites, and may even be a tool for detecting early-stage breast cancer, as Alix Ehlers and Elizabeth Thompson explain.
item.dc:title: Where in the world is whitlockite
item.dc:creator: Alix M. Ehlers
Elizabeth C. Thompson

item.title: Ice clouds born from Martian waves
item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02109-8

Water-ice clouds are common across the Solar System, but their formation typically requires pre-existing dust particles to coax water vapour into ice. Atmospheric simulations now suggest that gravity waves over a Martian volcano can bypass the need for dust, generating ice clouds through spontaneous nucleation of water vapour.
item.dc:title: Ice clouds born from Martian waves
item.dc:creator: Milena Corcos

item.title: Atmospheric lessons from Mars
item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02128-5

Despite its thin, carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere, Mars is proving a valuable laboratory for understanding atmospheric transport, cloud formation, and climate processes on Earth and beyond.
item.dc:title: Atmospheric lessons from Mars

item.title: Rethinking Agulhas Leakage impacts on Atlantic circulation
item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02111-0

The Agulhas Leakage is a set of currents that carry salty water from the Indian to the Atlantic Ocean around the southern tip of Africa. It helps drive modern Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, but evidence suggests this link wasn’t present in the Pliocene.
item.dc:title: Rethinking Agulhas Leakage impacts on Atlantic circulation
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Petrick

item.title: Homogeneous ice nucleation from water vapour suggested by elongated clouds on Mars
item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02089-9

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud on Mars probably forms by homogeneous ice nucleation, with implications for other planets including Earth and Venus, according to a model of homogeneous ice nucleation from water vapour in a meteorological model of Mars.
item.dc:title: Homogeneous ice nucleation from water vapour suggested by elongated clouds on Mars
item.dc:creator: J. Hernández-Bernal
A. Määttänen
A. Spiga
F. Forget
